**Nobel Prize in Physics (2010 – 2015)**  

| Year | Laureates | Brief description of the work that earned the prize |
|------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **2010** | **Andre Geï (Kazakhstan/Netherlands)** and **Konstantin Novoselov (Russia/UK)** | For the groundbreaking experiments that **isolated a single layer of carbon atoms – graphene** and demonstrated its extraordinary electronic, mechanical and optical properties. Their work opened a new field of research and paved the way for a host of potential applications (high‑speed transistors, flexible displays, sensors, etc.). |
| **2011** | **Saul Perlmutter** (USA) – **Brian P. Schmidt** (USA) – **Adam G. Riess** (USA) | Recognised for the discovery that the **expansion of the Universe is accelerating**. By observing distant Type Ia supernovae, they provided the first solid evidence for a repulsive form of energy now called **dark energy**, fundamentally changing cosmology. |
| **2012** | **Serge Haroche** (France) – **David J. Wineland** (USA) | Awarded for **experimental methods that enable the precise measurement and manipulation of individual quantum systems**. Haroche’s cavity‑QED experiments trapped photons; Wineland’s ion‑trap techniques controlled single atoms. Their work laid the experimental foundation for quantum information processing and ultra‑precise atomic clocks. |
| **2013** | **François Englert** (Belgium) – **Peter Higgs** (UK) | For the **theoretical discovery of a mechanism that gives mass to elementary particles** (the Higgs mechanism) and the prediction of the Higgs boson. The particle was later observed at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (2012), confirming the theory that underpins the Standard Model of particle physics. |
| **2014** | **Isamu Akasaki** (Japan) – **Hiroshi Amano** (Japan) – **Shuji Nakamura** (Japan/USA) | For the **invention of efficient blue light‑emitting diodes (LEDs)**. Their work made possible bright, long‑lasting white light sources and displays, dramatically reducing energy consumption for lighting worldwide. |
| **2015** | **Takaaki Kajita** (Japan) – **Arthur B. McDonald** (Canada) | Recognised for the **discovery of neutrino oscillations**, which shows that neutrinos have mass. Kajita’s Super‑Kamiokande experiment and McDonald’s Sudbury Neutrino Observatory independently demonstrated that neutrinos change “flavor” as they travel, a breakthrough that required revisions to the Standard Model of particle physics. |

These six years highlight a variety of breakthroughs—from new materials and quantum control to fundamental insights about the cosmos and the elementary particles that compose it.
